Voice & Calls
⏱ 4 min read📅 December 10, 2026✍️ custovox.ai

Mobile calls are declining. Customer service calls matter more

Mobile phones are used less and less for phone calls. Messaging apps and internet calls have taken over a large share of everyday conversations. Data from Statista Market Insights, published in 2023, confirms it: mobile voice revenue is in steady decline and is expected to stay that way.

For customer service, this decline might look like good news. In fact it is the opposite: the calls that remain are the ones that matter most.

A market in steady decline

According to Statista Market Insights, worldwide mobile voice revenue, meaning call services billed by carriers, fell from about $396.6 billion in 2016 to $264.4 billion in 2022. It was estimated at $257.8 billion in 2023.

Forecasts point to an average annual decline of 2.72% between 2023 and 2028, reaching about $224.6 billion in 2028. In 2022, mobile voice still accounted for 18.89% of the communication services market.

An important clarification: these figures measure carrier revenue, not the number of calls. They include voice services over mobile networks but exclude calls through internet apps.

Strong differences between regions

Asia remains the largest regional market, with about $103.7 billion in revenue in 2022. Among countries, the United States came first that year with about $49.4 billion.

Forecasts point to a decline in almost every region by 2028. The trend is therefore global: the phone stays in every pocket, but it is used less and less for routine calls.

Regions decline at different rates, but none is an exception to the overall trend.

For companies that serve customers internationally, the shift is the same everywhere: fewer routine calls, more calls that really count.

People call less, but when it matters

This decline mechanically changes the nature of calls. Routine exchanges move to writing. The calls that remain are the ones where writing is not enough: a complex situation, an urgent problem, a worry, a dispute.

For customer service, every call therefore carries higher stakes. A customer who picks up the phone has often already tried something else. They are more involved, sometimes more tense, and expect a real solution.

It is not a dying channel: according to a 2022 survey published by Statista, 54% of Americans still preferred the phone to resolve a problem with customer service.

The same logic applies to every company with a customer service line: fewer calls overall does not mean less work, but more demanding work on each call.

Richer conversations, rarely analyzed

These calls are the richest conversations in the customer relationship. Customers explain their situation in detail, in their own words and tone. You can hear frustration, urgency, trust or distrust.

Yet most companies use only a tiny fraction of them. A few calls are listened to again for quality control; the rest stay in recording systems nobody looks at. The most valuable information is also the least used.

This is all the more regrettable because these calls often come at decisive moments: just before a cancellation, after an incident, or when a contract is up for renewal. Not listening means missing those moments.

Customers, for their part, remember how a call went far longer than they remember an email.

Understanding every call

Today's tools can transcribe calls automatically and analyze them like text: reason for contact, emotions expressed, signs a customer may leave, commitments made. Automatic language analysis processes every call, not a sample.

That is what our VoiceIQ module does, in five languages, with models such as Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case. Data stays hosted in France and is never used to train models.

Managers then know why their customers really call, and which calls deserve particular attention.

The same analysis applies to recordings you already have, so there is no need to wait for new calls to start learning.

Results are grouped by topic and by week, so trends are easy to follow.

The takeaway

Mobile voice is declining, but customer service calls are not losing importance. They are gaining it. Fewer of them are about routine matters; they concentrate on the moments when the relationship is decided. Understanding all of them becomes a decisive advantage.

To get started, analyzing one month of calls is often enough: recurring reasons and moments of tension appear quickly, and show where to act first.
